quote: "Nowhere can man find a quieter or more untroubled retreat than in his own soul, above all when he has within him such thoughts that by looking into them he is immediately at perfect ease." — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV
context:
Marcus wrote the Meditations for no reader but himself, in army camps along the Danube, during years of plague and border war. He had every reason to look outward, toward the frontier and the crisis. Instead he kept returning to the counsel that the things worth finding are usually already present, unnoticed because something louder stands in front of them. His discipline was attention: to stop scanning the horizon and look at what was there all along.

This week astronomers reported something in that same spirit. 
Four nearby white dwarf stars were found hiding in plain sight beside brighter red dwarf companions, revealed by Hubble's ultraviolet observations, including one just 25 light-years away that took nearly three decades to confirm.
 
Seen in visible light there was only the red dwarf; the white dwarf, hotter at its surface, showed up only in the ultraviolet.
 The dead star was never absent. We were simply looking in the wrong light.
question: What is standing quietly beside the bright thing you keep looking at, waiting for you to change the light you see it by?
